episode.throughLine: After a rejected submission, a young doctor seeks a colleague's help, reaches another audience, and continues research whose questions are not settled by one experiment.

contentProfile.contentNote: Includes professional rejection and a brief, non-procedural account of risky self-experimentation and illness.

dramatizationLimits: No self-experiment method, amounts, culture protocol or medical advice.
No invented reactions, gestures, dialogue, ridicule or claims that every expert rejected the idea.
HOLD: turn combines documented steps whose precise timing is not fixed; final reading review required.
avoidRules: Do not claim the experiment caused or proved an ulcer.
Do not interpret rejection as evidence of being right.
Do not erase Warren, McGechie, Skirrow, hospital support or other researchers.
Do not claim the 1983 letter ranked the paper last or near last.

arc.canonicalText: A young doctor went to see a colleague at his hospital about a rejection letter. He was thirty-one. He and another doctor had been studying bacteria found in patients' tissue samples. They thought the bacteria might help explain an illness they treated. They had submitted their work to a meeting of specialists. The meeting was being held in their own city. That mattered when travel cost more than they could easily afford. But the letter said their work had not been accepted. He brought the problem to a colleague.
arc.sourceNote: Shared hospital encounter across scene, dark and response, from the 2008 memory. No invented office, hand movement, letter-reading location or dialogue. Age from letter date plus birth date.

arc.canonicalText: He remembered the rejection as the hardest day of the dispute. The letter itself was polite. It thanked him for sending the work. It said that many papers had been submitted and most had been accepted. His was among those left out. It described a committee choosing without knowing who had written each paper. It suggested that he might submit again after colleagues had examined the work. Those were possibilities for another submission. This meeting had turned him down. The page ended with a formal sign-off. There was no place for his talk.
arc.sourceNote: Low point is explicitly remembered, not an invented illness scene. Letter wording is paraphrased without asserting hostile motive, rank, or bias. The formal sign-off is visible in figure 3.

arc.canonicalText: He went to the doctor who was supervising him. The man worked with bacteria. He had been growing these bacteria too. He could see that they were there. The young doctor had reached someone with direct experience of the work. In his memory, that was who he approached after the letter arrived. He had gone to another person.
arc.sourceNote: First documented small act is seeking a colleague after rejection. No risky experiment as the reader's model. The wording does not invent an explicit request or a reply beyond the remembered encounter.

arc.canonicalText: Before that letter, the work had included long stretches of failure. They had seen the bacteria in tissue but had struggled to grow them. The early attempts had produced no culture they could study. Eventually, they succeeded. They also collected information from patients undergoing examination. Bacteria appeared alongside inflammation and ulcers in the results. That association was a reason to investigate. It did not, by itself, establish what caused what. Meanwhile, the young doctor still had patients and training duties. He fitted the research around them. He took the references with him when his job moved him far away. There he worked through the results and prepared them to be presented. The rejected submission had come after that work.
arc.sourceNote: Explicit backward jump, compressed chronology. First culture in 1982 is retrospective; association is contemporaneous study evidence. No laboratory recipe or procedural quantities. The failed effort receives space without attributing ignorance or malice.

arc.canonicalText: In his later account, his colleague answered with encouragement. The colleague was growing the bacteria too. He could see that they were real. He thought the work had a future. This was support from someone examining the same problem. It was not proof that every claim was right. He had heard an encouraging answer.
arc.sourceNote: The turn is the encouragement Marshall remembered receiving during the McGechie conversation. It is not a new bodily reaction, guaranteed vindication, or a claim that travel logistics happened in that encounter. Memory remains probable. Subsequent practical arrangements are compressed in became.

arc.canonicalText: His later autobiography describes the arrangements that followed. His colleague supplied a contact. Another researcher arranged a presentation at a European meeting. A travel grant helped make the trip possible. He traveled to the meeting. During that trip, another group also found the bacteria in a patient's sample. More people were working on the question. But the following year still brought rejected papers and experiments that failed. He also carried out a risky experiment on himself and became ill. The result added evidence that the bacteria could inflame the stomach. It did not establish that he had given himself an ulcer. He recovered from the acute illness. By the end of the year, he had funding for a controlled treatment study. He moved hospitals to reach enough patients for it. There was another study to do.
arc.sourceNote: Later arrangements are not staged inside the earlier conversation. The 2008 interview recalls McGechie calling; the autobiography describes supplied contact details. The drama uses the latter account, without asserting both as one instant action. Endpoint end1984. Original 1985 abstract supports illness/gastritis and limits, not dosing or treatment advice. No instant vindication. No quantity, method, protocol or claim of deliberate poisoning. Recovery follows abstract's temporary illness, not seed's simplistic self-cure claim.

arc.canonicalText:
His name was Barry Marshall.

He and a colleague discovered how stomach bacteria contribute to ulcers.

Your life is not theirs.

But a piece of this story may still sit beside you.

You are allowed to ask for another perspective.

You do not have to be certain.
arc.sourceNote: No claim that rejection proves correctness or that self-experimentation is admirable advice.
